explain: Every terminal line has the same shape: the command (what), flags (how, starting with -), and arguments (on what).
Flags: short ones use one - and can be joined (-la). Long ones use two -- and a word.
remember: One dash, one letter; two dashes, a whole word.

explain: Paths: / separates folders, ~ is your home, . is here, .. is one folder up.

syntax:
echo "hi" > note.txt
echo "more" >> note.txt
cat note.txt | wc -l
explain: Plumbing: > sends output into a file (replace), >> adds to it, | sends one command's output into the next.
remember: > pour into a file, | pass to the next.

explain: grep = command, -rn = two flags (recursive, line numbers), then two arguments: what to look for and where.
remember: Split any long command at the spaces: command, flags, arguments.

explain: A pipeline: four small commands joined with |. Each does one job on the last one's output.
Print working directory: shows which folder you are in.
example: Checking where you are before running a command.

explain: Lists files. -l shows details, -a includes hidden files (names starting with a dot).
example: Seeing everything in a project folder, including .gitignore.

explain: cd changes folder. ~ is your home folder, .. goes up one level. Try it in the practice terminal.
example: Moving into your project before running npm start.

explain: mkdir makes a folder. touch makes an empty file.

syntax:
cp notes.txt backup.txt
mv backup.txt old-notes.txt
explain: cp copies a file. mv moves or renames it.
Deletes a file right away. It does not go to the Trash, so double-check first.
example: Cleaning up files you are sure you no longer need.

explain: Makes a file executable, so you can run it with ./run.sh.
Searches for text in every file under this folder. -r goes into subfolders, -n shows line numbers.
example: Finding every TODO note in your code.

syntax:
git status
git add .
git commit -m "Add notes"
git push
explain: See what changed, stage it, save a commit with a message, and upload it.
example: Saving and publishing your website changes.

explain: ls lists files. -l shows details. Add a folder name to look inside it.
.. goes up one folder, ~ goes home, - goes back to where you just were.
Paths: ~ is your home folder, / separates folders.

syntax:
open .
open notes.txt
open -a "Visual Studio Code" .
explain: open opens a folder in Finder or a file in its app. -a picks the app.
example: Opening a project in VS Code.

explain: touch makes empty files (or updates the time on existing ones).
-p makes all the folders in the path, even if the parents don't exist yet.
example: Making nested folders in one go.

explain: cat prints a whole file. less shows it page by page (q quits).

syntax:
head -n 5 notes.txt
tail -n 5 notes.txt
tail -f server.log
explain: head shows the start, tail the end. tail -f keeps showing new lines as they're added.
example: Watching a log while a server runs.

explain: wc counts. -l counts lines.
> writes into a file (replacing it). >> adds to the end.

syntax:
mv draft.txt final.txt
mv final.txt Documents/
explain: mv renames a file, or moves it into a folder.
-r means "the folder and everything in it". Be careful: rm does not use the Trash.
ln -s makes a shortcut (symbolic link) to a file.
example: Using one file from two places.

explain: nano is a simple text editor inside the terminal. Ctrl+O saves, Ctrl+X quits.
find searches folders for files by name. * matches anything.
example: Finding every .txt file in a project.

explain: -i ignores upper/lower case, -c counts matching lines.

syntax:
ls | wc -l
cat names.txt | sort | uniq
history | grep git
explain: | sends one command's output into the next command.
&& runs the next command only if the first one worked.
example: Only push when the tests pass.

explain: whoami your user name, date the time, which shows where a program lives.
example: Checking which Python you are using.

explain: man shows the manual for a command (q quits).
example: Learning what flags a command has.

explain: history lists commands you typed. clear wipes the screen. ↑ brings back the last command.
du shows how big files and folders are, df how much disk space is free. -h means human-readable.

syntax:
ps aux | grep node
kill 12345
top
explain: ps lists running programs, kill stops one by its number (PID), top shows live CPU use (q quits).
Shows which program is using port 3000.

syntax:
curl https://api.github.com
curl -O https://example.com/file.zip
ping -c 3 google.com
explain: curl downloads from a URL (-O saves the file). ping checks if a site answers.
example: Testing an API, checking the internet.

explain: 7 = read+write+run for you, 5 = read+run for others. ls -l shows the permissions.
sudo runs a command as the admin. It asks for your password. Only use it when you trust the command.
PATH is the list of folders where the terminal looks for programs.
alias makes a shortcut. Put it in ~/.zshrc to keep it, then source reloads the file.
./ runs a program in this folder. Or give the script to bash.

syntax:
Ctrl+C    stop the running command
Ctrl+A    jump to the start of the line
Ctrl+E    jump to the end of the line
Ctrl+R    search your history
Tab       finish a file name for you
explain: Keyboard shortcuts that save a lot of typing.
init starts a new repository here. clone downloads an existing one.

syntax:
git add .
git commit -m "Add contact page"
git push
explain: add picks changes, commit saves them with a message, push uploads them.

syntax:
git pull
git log --oneline
git diff
explain: pull downloads new changes, log shows history, diff shows what you changed.
example: Staying up to date with the team.

syntax:
git branch
git switch -c new-feature
git switch main
git merge new-feature
explain: Branches let you try things without breaking main. merge brings the work back.

syntax:
git restore index.html
git stash
git stash pop
explain: restore throws away changes to a file. stash hides changes for later; pop brings them back.
